en: 1. Regarding the *Sūtra on Protecting One’s Life*:
one believes in the Buddha’s sublime Dharma and receives its training without forgetting it. 2. One does not covet worldly glory and severs mundane causes and conditions.
3. One vows to practice noble wisdom for the protection of all beings. 4. One vows to gather the assembly.
Ninth, wherever one is reborn,
one shall always vow to encounter a Buddha.
Tenth, one shall uphold the prohibitive precepts and extensively deliver all living beings.
Eleventh, to study extensively and master various wisdoms in order to proclaim them to the fourfold assembly.
Twelfth, to constantly vow to meet with the Buddhas in every lifetime, extensively expound the essentials of the Path, and deliver immeasurable beings.
These are the twelve noble insights.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If there are bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, princes, or palace ladies..."
Those who are able to practice these twelve dharmas will,
wherever they are reborn, always encounter a Buddha.
As they travel about to teach and transform others, they shall long remain free from all suffering and enter the three dharma-gates, whereby their merit shall be fully accomplished.
One swiftly attains Buddhahood while still traversing the three realms;
being free from all obstructions, none can sever this path.
Having practiced this matter for five previous lifetimes, one personally achieves Buddhahood.
If there are kings, ministers, elders, members of the royal harem and their retinues, as well as good sons and good daughters among the fourfold assembly of disciples,
who desire to seek this unsurpassed path in order to extensively deliver all beings;
Those who wish to seek the Dharma of the Three Vehicles should also read this sutra. Those who wish to seek the Dharma of the Three Vehicles should also read this sutra.
Those who seek to transcend the world early and attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) should also read this sutra.
Those who seek to be reborn in the sublime and blissful heavens above should also read it.
One should also read this sutra.
Those who wish to seek the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King should also read this sutra.
Those who seek noble status and wealth should also read this sutra.
If there are women who seek a male body, they too should do so.
One should also read this sutra.
Those who wish to be constantly accompanied by and taught by an enlightened master in every lifetime should also read this sutra.
All those who have such vows and desires should read this sutra;
this sutra is sublime and powerful.
Any son or daughter of good family who is able to receive, uphold,
and practice this sutra will always be protected by the majestic spiritual power of all the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions,
and they will also be protected by the seven Buddhas of the past.
It is also protected by the various honored Bodhisattvas and great disciples;
furthermore, by the devas, nāgas, spirits, the sun and moon, the five planets, the twenty-eight lunar mansions, and all the honored celestial deities.
They shall always follow and protect those who read this sutra,
ensuring that they never meet with an untimely death,
and that no malevolent spirits whatsoever can cause them harm.
Because these good men and good women practice the path of the bodhisattva,
all the sages of the ten directions together protect and watch over them.
The merit of those who read this sutra is immeasurable.
The Buddha’s words are not dualistic.
Those who hear this sutra,
those who receive and uphold it, and those who copy it down— [they shall all attain liberation].
All your wishes shall be fulfilled.
Ānanda, listen attentively, listen attentively, and uphold this sutra.
Diligently teach all people to receive, study, recite, and read it.
"Do not forget or fall away from this.
Ānanda immediately replied,
"I shall receive the teaching of the World-Honored One."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra,
there was among those seated a daughter of an elder named Shanxin (Good Faith), who,
together with five hundred companions, rose from their seats all at once.
Prostrating with his five limbs touching the Buddha’s feet,
he knelt for a long time and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, women such as Śrī are beset by the defilements of sin."
"Having received the Buddha's compassionate grace, I have been able to hear the sublime Dharma.
I do not regard my status as a lowly woman as a hindrance; I wish to become your disciple.
The Buddha said:
Welcome, all you women.
You possess the merit from past lives to have encountered a Buddha;
those who delight in hearing the Dharma truly attain liberation from suffering.
In all future births, she shall be far removed from the female body.
Having received the five precepts from the Buddha, she became a laywoman of pure faith (*upāsikā*).
The entire assembly was filled with joy.
Each of them then placed their heads upon the ground and received the five precepts.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"These virtuous female lay followers have long been born into this world."
Before hearing the Buddha and before hearing the Dharma,
one was regarded with suspicion by the Teacher of Enmity;
following worldly conditions, one may even destroy the True Dharma.
Some destroy stupas and monasteries;
some kill true persons;
some misappropriate the property of the Triple Gem.
Some kill their parents;
some commit offenses against the multitude;
they possess no self-awakened wisdom.
The multitude of transgressions I have committed are beyond measure;
now that I have been able to see the Buddha,
my mind has opened and my understanding has been resolved.
Realizing that their past conduct was wrong,
they and their peers developed faith; from this day forward,
they shall reform their lives, cultivate themselves, and reverently uphold the honored precepts of the Buddha.
"And may we uphold this sutra,
remaining free from transgression in every lifetime.
We pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will grant us the five precepts."
The Buddha told the women:
"Listen attentively and uphold this:
first, maintain benevolence by not killing, extending kindness to all living beings."
Second, guarding one’s integrity by not stealing and using what one possesses to relieve the masses;
third, maintaining purity by refraining from sexual misconduct so as to remain untainted;
fourth, ensuring speech is not frivolous or deceitful, thereby avoiding verbal transgressions.
Fifth, by staying far from wine and not drinking it, one avoids committing many offenses and incurring resentment.
One should observe the precepts of the fast, constantly practice great compassion,
and offer prayers for all beings while reverently practicing the words of the Buddha.
Never shall you regret this midway.
Exerting all that you are capable of, it is better to die upholding the good than to live by violating the enemy.
You all must come and uphold the prohibitive precepts of the Buddha.
Praised by all the devas,
he did not follow worldly customs of false delusion, nor did he prostrate before spirits or deities; rather,
he guarded the prohibitive precepts as if his head were on fire.
Sitting, one observes the body for oneself:
its form will not endure,
and its appearance will not remain.
Life is like the wind; when one encounters even slight illness, it is like being trapped in a sack.
Do not harbor indulgence or dwell in resentful conduct.
All things are impermanent.
One should establish diligence and abandon worldly thoughts.
Just as a bodhisattva practices, one should resolve the mind according to one's vows.
What does one seek to attain in this life and in future lives?
As they wish, they shall all obtain their goals; it shall never be in vain.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If you and others protect and practice [this teaching], you may attain Buddhahood."
The Buddha-way must be studied;
the sutras and dharmas must be read.
That I have now attained Buddhahood is solely due to the accumulation of study.
In this sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna,
there is neither male nor female, neither noble nor base;
for whoever hears this sutra, [there is no distinction].
Protected by the empowerment of all Buddhas,
all their aspirations shall be fully realized.
When the Buddha spoke this sutra, [all present attained realization].
Devas, nāgas, spirits, ghosts, kings, humans, and the fourfold assembly of disciples— numbering three hundred million—
saw the Buddha preach this sutra;
they all rejoiced greatly and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Each of them gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment.
They then prostrated themselves with their heads to the ground in salutation and respectfully received [the teaching].
The Buddha told Ānanda:
Listen attentively and receive this teaching; uphold, widely proclaim, and disseminate it,
so that all sentient beings of embodied form may receive,
uphold, read, recite, transcribe, and make offerings to it.
The essential Dharma of the Buddha can eliminate the most grievous sins of incalculable kalpas;
it can deliver immeasurable, boundless, and asankhyeya sentient beings, causing them all to attain liberation.
This sutra has issued from the very mouth of the Buddha.
Should there be anyone who reads even a single sentence or a single verse and praises it,
no heterodox influences that oppose the Way or any malevolent ghosts shall be able to approach them.
Their lifespan shall be truly long, and they shall never meet with an untimely death;
whatever they seek, they shall obtain entirely according to their wishes.
While this sutra was being spoken, [the assembly rejoiced].
The entire great assembly, along with the dragons, spirits, and the four classes of disciples,
prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and,
receiving the teachings of the Celestial Honored One, single-mindedly put them into practice.

On the fifteenth day of the twelfth month of the second year of the Zhengguang era, the lay devotee Zhang Ayi transcribed this *Hu shenming jing* (Sūtra on Protecting One’s Life and Spirit) for the purpose of receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and making offerings to it,
[thereby benefiting] himself and his parents for seven generations back.
From those below up to one's own person, all are the path of sincere and wholesome contemplation.
